title: True entrusting
hookLine: faith as entrusting oneself, not as belief forced by effort
last: OTHER POWER: EVEN THE TRUST IS GIVEN.

cards: A disciple brings his teacher an awkward confession. When I say the nembutsu, he says, I don't feel joy leaping up inside me the way I'm told I should. And I'm in no hurry at all to go to the Pure Land.

What's wrong with me? A teacher could scold him, or tell him to try harder. In the record called the Tannisho, the disciple is Yuien, the teacher is Shinran, and Shinran answers: I have wondered the very same thing.
Today's word is what Shinran says is still there, under the missing joy: shinjin.

teach.h: NOT GRIPPING: LETTING YOURSELF BE HELD.
teach.b: First, the word. Shinjin is often translated faith, but in English faith can sound like believing something hard enough, gripping a claim with your will. Some Shin translators render shinjin as true entrusting instead.
Not gripping: letting yourself be held. Second, where it comes from. For Shinran, shinjin is not something you produce.
Following other power all the way through, he taught that the entrusting heart is itself given by Amida, the Buddha's own mind awakened in an ordinary one.
You can't force it into being, any more than you can force yourself to fall asleep. Third, back to Yuien's confession.
In the Tannisho, Shinran says the missing joy is the work of our cravings and passions, the very things that hold us back.

teach.h: THE VOW WAS MADE FOR PEOPLE LIKE THIS.
teach.b: Then he turns it around: the vow was made precisely for people like this. If we felt nothing but eager joy, we might wonder whether we had any passions left at all. The doubt doesn't disqualify the disciple.
It shows him who the vow is for. Fourth, what entrusting looks like.

teach.h: A CHILD ASLEEP IN THE BACK SEAT.
teach.b: One way to picture it: a child who has stopped fighting sleep in the back seat on a long drive. The child isn't believing hard that the driver is good.
The child has simply stopped keeping watch. That letting go isn't lazy; it's a kind of honesty about who is really driving. Shinjin, in Shinran's teaching, is not a feeling to work up.
It's a weight finally set down.

how: In Jodo Shinshu, shinjin is understood as the entrusting heart given by Amida; Shin Buddhists hear it explained in temple talks and readings from Shinran and the Tannisho, and say the nembutsu as its expression rather than as a way to produce it.

o: true entrusting, a trust given by Amida, not forced
a feeling of leaping joy each time you chant

games.q: you're Shinran. a disciple confesses he feels no joy when he says the name, and no hurry to reach the Pure Land. what do you say?
o: you must try harder to feel it.
I have wondered the same thing.
then you should stop saying the name.
games.why: Shinran admits the same doubt, then says the vow was made for people with passions just like these.

practice: Bring up one worry that's been riding with you, something you can't fix today, and name it plainly in a few words. Instead of solving it, picture setting it down on a table, or in open hands, and taking your hands away.
If you pray, hand it over the way your tradition does; if not, just practice not holding it for now. If it climbs back up, set it down again.

wordCard.voice: Shinjin. True entrusting: in Shinran's teaching, a trust that is given by Amida rather than forced by effort. Today's word.

orig.note: Japanese: shinjin, often rendered faith; some Shin translators say true entrusting.

carryVoice: Your line: entrusted. The child in the back seat has stopped keeping watch. I'll be here tomorrow.
